name: addr2line (gimli-rs)
baseline: GNU binutils addr2line (also compared: elfutils eu-addr2line and llvm-addr2line)
workload: Wall time of resolving batches of random addresses (addr2line -af -e) in four large debug-info files: Firefox libxul.so.debug (500 queries), clangd-18.debug (500), mold.debug (1000) and postgres.debug (10000), timed with hyperfine and drawn as a bar chart.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Current benchmarks show a performance improvement in all cases' versus binutils addr2line, eu-addr2line and llvm-addr2line. The magnitudes exist only as bars in benchmark-time.svg; the README and the plotting script give no numeric values, so no ratio is stated here.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --features bin, run through scripts/benchmark-addr2line-docker.sh (builds a Docker image named opensuse-addr2line and runs scripts/benchmark-addr2line.sh); baseline tools are the image's /usr/bin addr2line, llvm-addr2line and eu-addr2line, versions not stated
tradeoffs: Rust library with a small CLI that implements only part of the GNU addr2line options; trades memory for speed by caching parsed DWARF (README: 'optimizes for speed over memory'); callable from C++ only through an FFI wrapper.
caveats: Numbers appear only in an SVG bar chart (no values, no CPU model, hyperfine run with --min-runs=1); the SVG metadata shows it was generated 2024-08-06, so tool versions date from then. First-party benchmark, and the README itself says the library 'aims to perform similarly' to the existing tools. Benchmark script is public, so the chart can be regenerated.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than objdump" OR "faster than readelf" OR "faster than addr2line" OR "faster than binutils" tool benchmark' returned the docs.rs addr2line README; then opened the repo, scripts/benchmark-addr2line.sh and benchmark-time.svg

name: Intel XED (x86 encoder decoder)
workload: Decode-only and decode+format throughput in MB/s over the 77 MB x86-64 code section of Firefox 86.0.1 xul.dll, one shootout of nine x86 disassembler libraries.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: XED 55.39 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19 and bddisasm 35.48 MB/s (about 1.62x and 1.56x, derived from page data). Decode+format: XED 15.67 MB/s vs Capstone 14.02 MB/s (about 1.12x, derived from page data). XED is slower than iced, yaxpeax and diStorm in both tables, slower than udis86 80.72 and Zydis (min) 61.33 MB/s in decode only, and slower than Zydis 22.24 and bddisasm 16.00 MB/s in decode+format.
compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, Rust 1.52.1; make-all.sh builds XED with mfile.py --no-encoder --opt=3 --extra-flags=-flto and Capstone as a Release build with -flto
tradeoffs: Intel's own IA32/Intel64 encoder and decoder library; built with a Python-based build system (mfile.py/mbuild); the benchmark builds it decoder-only. Other libraries in the same table are several times faster.
caveats: Margin over Capstone is small (1.12x, derived) and XED sits mid-table, so this is a weak win. The shootout is run by the iced maintainers, a competitor, in a fork of athre0z/disas-bench; XED's own README makes no speed claim. Capstone cannot run decode-only, so no decode-only ratio against it. Measurements are from 2021 on a 2015-era desktop CPU. The other winners of this shootout (iced, yaxpeax-x86, diStorm, Zydis, bddisasm) are reported by the other wave 13 asmtool searches.
found_via: WebSearch 'x86 disassembler decoder speed comparison blog XED Zydis Capstone iced benchmark results MB/s' led to disas-bench; opened icedland/disas-bench README (results tables) and make-all.sh

name: udis86
baseline: Zydis, bddisasm and Intel XED (decode only); it loses to Capstone and Zydis in decode+format
workload: Decode-only throughput in MB/s over the 77 MB x86-64 code section of Firefox 86.0.1 xul.dll in the disas-bench shootout of nine x86 disassembler libraries.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: udis86 80.72 MB/s vs Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48 and XED 55.39 MB/s (about 2.36x, 2.28x and 1.46x, derived from page data); diStorm 92.17, yaxpeax 182.08 and iced 256.69 MB/s are faster. Decode+format: udis86 12.02 MB/s, slower than Capstone 14.02 MB/s and Zydis 22.24 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0; make-all.sh builds udis86 with ./configure --enable-static=yes and no LTO (comment: LTO makes the build extremely slow), while Capstone, Zydis, bddisasm, XED and diStorm are built with -flto
tradeoffs: Old, abandoned library; README lists MMX, x87, 3DNow, SSE through SSE4.2, AES, AMD-V, VMX and SMX and does not mention AVX or AVX-512, so it cannot decode current code; decoder tables are generated with Python scripts; slowest formatter in the shootout (12.02 MB/s decode+format, below BeaEngine's 13.42).
caveats: The decode-only lead probably reflects its much narrower instruction coverage as well as its design, and it loses in decode+format. Shootout run by the iced maintainers (a competitor) in 2021, with LTO disabled for udis86 only. Last commit December 2014. The page does not check that every decode-only row decodes the whole test file correctly.
found_via: Harvested from the icedland/disas-bench results table (surfaced by WebSearch 'x86 disassembler decoder speed comparison blog XED Zydis Capstone iced benchmark results MB/s'); opened vmt/udis86 and its commits page

name: B2R2 (binary analysis framework, disassembler front-end)
baseline: Capstone, through Capstone.NET (C#) and the Capstone Python binding
workload: Seconds to disassemble three raw binary blobs taken from default Linux distributions (blob_x86, blob_x86_64, libc_x86); each number is the mean of 10 runs, lower is better.
claimed_speedup: Average over the three blobs: B2R2 17.748 s vs Capstone.NET 78.835 s and Capstone Python 82.172 s (about 4.44x and 4.63x, derived from page data). Per blob: blob_x86 28.298 vs 127.847 s, blob_x86_64 24.317 vs 106.414 s, libc_x86 0.63 vs 2.245 s. Iced (C#) is faster than B2R2 (15.737 s average).
compiler_and_flags: dotnet run -c release for each .NET project (SDK version not stated); B2R2 v0.5.0; Capstone Python run as 'python capstone_test_python.py'
tradeoffs: Managed .NET (F#) framework, not usable from C++ without hosting the CLR; the disassembler is one part of a binary analysis framework that also lifts to IR and recovers control-flow graphs.
caveats: Comparison repo is run by the B2R2 authors; no CPU, OS or .NET version is given. The baseline is Capstone through managed or Python bindings, so binding marshalling overhead is included and the ratio overstates the gap to native Capstone. Numbers are for B2R2 v0.5.0 (comparison repo last updated 2021-10-23); the framework has changed a lot since. No license is stated on the comparison repo page. B2R2 is slower than Iced in the same table.
found_via: WebSearch 'x86 disassembler decoder speed comparison blog XED Zydis Capstone iced benchmark results MB/s' returned B2R2-org/DisasmComparison; opened its README and commits page

name: Keystone Engine
baseline: LLVM MC assembler (llvm-mc / the LLVM build it was derived from)
workload: Footprint of the assembler engine (binary size and memory consumption) and time to build the project, compared with LLVM, from which Keystone's MC-based core was stripped down.
claimed_speedup: docs/beyond_llvm.md: Keystone is 'more than 10 times smaller in size and in memory consumption' than LLVM, and 'Initial verson of Keystone takes only 30 seconds to compile on a laptop, while LLVM needs 15 minutes to build'.
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars; bindings for Python, Rust, Go, Java and others
tradeoffs: Dual licence: GPL-2.0 (with a client exceptions file) or a paid commercial licence. Multi-architecture assembler framework (Arm, Arm64, Hexagon, Mips, PowerPC, Sparc, SystemZ, X86) with a small C API, but built on a modified copy of LLVM MC rather than the current LLVM tree.
caveats: Claim is about size, memory and build time, not assembly throughput, and gives no measurement method, LLVM version, flags or machine. First-party doc page that dates from the project's initial version. No assemble-time comparison with GNU as, NASM or llvm-mc is made anywhere in the repo.
found_via: WebSearch 'assembler "faster than Keystone" OR "faster than LLVM MC" OR "faster than llvm-mc" OR "faster than gas" github benchmark' surfaced docs/beyond_llvm.md; opened the repo page, commits page and the doc
